hints: Remember that a positive enthalpy change means endothermic (heat taken in), while a negative change means exothermic (heat given out).
Notice that process 1 is neutralisation to form water and process 2 is combustion of methane, both classic examples of heat-releasing reactions.
Consider what happens to energy when a gas condenses to a liquid in process 3, as particles come closer and form stronger attractions.
walkthrough:
**Recall what sign means**

Positive $\Delta H$ means endothermic, heat is absorbed from surroundings. Negative $\Delta H$ means exothermic, heat is released to surroundings.

$$\Delta H > 0 \text{ endothermic, } \Delta H < 0 \text{ exothermic}$$

**Check process 1 and process 2**

Process 1 is the neutralisation of $\text{H}^{+}(aq)$ with $\text{OH}^{-}(aq)$ to make $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}(l)$. Bond formation releases energy, so it is exothermic.

$$\text{H}^{+}(aq) + \text{OH}^{-}(aq) \rightarrow \text{H}_{2}\text{O}(l) \quad \Delta H < 0$$

**Check combustion**

Process 2 is the complete combustion of $\text{CH}_{4}(g)$. All combustions are exothermic because strong $\text{C=O}$ and $\text{O-H}$ bonds are formed.

$$\text{CH}_{4}(g) + 2\text{O}_{2}(g) \rightarrow \text{CO}_{2}(g) + 2\text{H}_{2}\text{O}(l) \quad \Delta H < 0$$

**Check condensation**

Process 3 is $\text{NH}_{3}(g) \rightarrow \text{NH}_{3}(l)$. Gas to liquid is condensation. Particles lose kinetic energy and form intermolecular attractions, so heat is released.

$$\text{gas} \rightarrow \text{liquid} \text{ is always exothermic, } \Delta H < 0$$

**Conclude**

All three processes have negative enthalpy changes. So none of them have a positive enthalpy change.

options.A: Correct. Process 1 (neutralisation), process 2 (combustion) and process 3 (condensation) are all exothermic with negative $\Delta H$. Therefore none have a positive enthalpy change.
options.B: Incorrect. Process 1 is neutralisation, which forms a covalent $\text{O-H}$ bond in water and releases heat. Students sometimes confuse ionic mixing in solution with an endothermic dissolving process, but this $\Delta H$ is negative.
options.C: Incorrect. Process 2 is combustion of methane, which is strongly exothermic. The trap is thinking that breaking $\text{C-H}$ and $\text{O=O}$ bonds needs energy, but far more energy is released when $\text{CO}_{2}$ and $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ form.
options.D: Incorrect. Process 3 is condensation, the reverse of vaporisation. Vaporisation (liquid to gas) is endothermic, but condensation (gas to liquid) is exothermic because intermolecular forces form and heat is given out.
